notes: Comprehensive review tracing the mammalian locomotor central pattern generator from Graham Brown's early experiments to modern spinal-cord work: a caudally localized spinal network autonomously generates the basic rhythm and pattern command signals to limb muscles, and homologous CPG networks govern walking, flying, and swimming across species. The review frames the CPG as the source of the basic locomotor command onto which descending and afferent control is layered.
animal_study: The review's localization claim can be tested by complete spinalization with pharmacological or peripheral-stimulus evocation of rhythmic motor output, comparing cervical, thoracic, and lumbar segments to verify that the rhythm- and pattern-generating network sits caudally in the cord.
robot_sim: Implement a spinal network that generates locomotor rhythm and pattern command signals with descending and sensory inputs removed; persistence of coordinated rhythmic motor output in the model tests the CPG-autonomy claim the review summarizes.

notes: A dual-lesion paradigm in cats shows the spinal CPG undergoes plastic changes after partial spinal cord injury that are shaped by locomotor training: cats trained on the treadmill after a partial thoracic lesion expressed bilateral hindlimb locomotion within hours of a subsequent complete transection, whereas untrained cats walked asymmetrically with the limb on the partially lesioned side recovering first. Re-expression of the hindlimb locomotor pattern after partial SCI therefore arises mostly from intrinsic changes below the lesion in the CPG and afferent inputs rather than from remnant descending pathways.
animal_study: Replicate the dual-lesion design while controlling training dose and timing to quantify how locomotor training sculpts CPG plasticity, and add dorsal-root section after the partial lesion to dissociate the afferent-input contribution from intrinsic CPG changes, which the abstract attributes jointly.
robot_sim: Model a spinal CPG whose synapses adapt during repetitive rhythmic 'training' activation, then remove descending drive completely; the trained network should re-express bilateral rhythm rapidly while the untrained network recovers slowly and asymmetrically, reproducing the lesion hierarchy.

notes: A neuromechanical model of the stick insect femur-tibia joint control network, run in-the-loop with a robotic limb, shows that the reflex reversal from resistance reflex to active reaction can be generated by inhibiting the network's flexion position and velocity afferents from the femoral chordotonal organ. Reflex reversal and limb-strain reinforcement (descending DUM neuron activation) are each necessary but individually insufficient to produce and maintain rhythmic stepping, which brief transient descending signals can initiate or halt, and removing parts of the feedback loop halts stepping independent of higher centers.
animal_study: In intact stick insects, selectively inhibit the processing of flexion position and velocity afferents from the femoral chordotonal organ during actual stepping to test the model's prediction that this inhibition alone converts the resistance reflex into the active reaction.
robot_sim: Implement the non-spiking interneuron joint-control network with chordotonal position and velocity afferents plus limb-strain reinforcement; separately ablate the afferent-inhibition pathway and the strain loop to reproduce the necessary-but-insufficient result for initiating and maintaining stepping.

notes: Chronic single-fiber recordings from L7 dorsal roots in unrestrained walking cats: spindle Ia primaries of ankle extensors fire fastest during the phase in which they are passively stretched, with fusimotor drive during active contraction insufficient to fully overcome the unloading effect of rapid shortening, and Ib tendon organs of toe extensors discharge mainly during stance with some swing-phase activity. Cycle-to-cycle firing variability was far higher during active contraction, and brisk muscle stretches evoked rapid (disynaptic or trisynaptic) reflex arcs, arguing that mesencephalic-preparation work had exaggerated alpha-gamma coactivation during normal stepping.
animal_study: Repeat identified single-afferent dorsal-root recordings across treadmill speeds and slopes with concurrent EMG to quantify how fusimotor drive and shortening-induced unloading shape Ia firing phase, targeting the high cycle-to-cycle variability observed during active contraction.
robot_sim: Implement spindle Ia models in which gamma drive biases firing but rapid shortening unloads the spindle, and Ib firing gated by stance loading; simulated afferent phase profiles can then be validated against these recorded discharge patterns during walking.
flags: Brisk stretch of ankle extensors evoked a rapid (disynaptic or trisynaptic) reflex arc in the conscious cat; no vocabulary entry covers a disynaptic/trisynaptic Ia stretch-reflex excitation, so feedback left empty - consider adding one.

notes: A connectionist CPG model of leaky-integrator neurons tuned by a genetic algorithm reproduces the salamander's aquatic traveling-wave swimming and terrestrial standing-wave trotting by coupling a lamprey-like body CPG with a limb CPG. Tonic, non-oscillating excitation applied to the single network modulates speed, direction, and gait type, demonstrating that one distributed circuit with two coupled subnetworks can underlie both locomotor programs.
animal_study: Test in salamander spinal preparations or with lesions whether the body and limb locomotor programs are organized as coupled but separable CPGs as the model assumes, for example whether disconnecting the limb CPG leaves the body-axis swimming wave intact.
robot_sim: Implement the two-level body-plus-limb CPG with a genetic-algorithm parameter search; sweep the tonic drive to verify gait, speed, and direction modulation, and ablate the limb-to-body CPG coupling to isolate the swimming program.

notes: An adaptive estimator model of human stance control dynamically weights the difference between expected and actual sensory signals as a function of estimated environmental conditions, with only sensor noise characteristics supplied by the designer. The model reproduces the saturation of visually induced sway and its absence in vestibular-loss subjects without any explicit vestibular threshold, and predicts that vestibular function is needed to prevent falling during sinusoidal support-base translations while loss of foot somatosensory information enlarges postural sway.
animal_study: The model's predictions map onto animal tests: bilateral vestibular lesion or foot somatosensory blockade during support-surface translations and large rotations with eyes closed would test whether sway enlargement and falls follow the estimator's predicted pattern.
robot_sim: Implement the adaptive sensory-error weighting estimator in a balance controller; removing the vestibular channel should reproduce the loss of visually-induced-sway saturation and the predicted falls in sensory-conflict conditions.
flags: Balance sensory-integration model (vestibular, visual, somatosensory weighting) lies outside the current afferent/feedback vocabulary; vestibular and visual inputs have no SADb tags.

notes: A hybrid Boolean framework models neural bursting activity and simple biomechanics faster than real time, yielding a multifunctional model of Aplysia feeding that qualitatively reproduces biting, swallowing, and rejection and switches behaviors in response to external sensory cues while incorporating known neural connectivity and a simple bioinspired periphery. Multifunctional real-time control can therefore emerge from one multifunctional circuit plus peripheral biomechanics rather than dedicated circuits per behavior.
animal_study: Use the model's qualitative behavioral-switching predictions to design in vivo tests in Aplysia, for example peripheral sensory stimulation at predicted transition points to probe whether a single network switches among the three feeding behaviors.
robot_sim: Implement the hybrid Boolean network with sensory-cued behavioral switching on a multifunctional robot task; ablate the connections the model predicts are essential for switching to test its hypothesis-generating claim.
flags: Aplysia californica (mollusk) is not in the animals vocabulary, so animals left empty - consider adding a Mollusk/Aplysia entry.

notes: In human walking, the knee moment-angle relationship is approximately linear within both the flexion and extension stages of stance, giving nearly constant quasi-stiffnesses that are well predicted (R2 > 86%) by gait speed, knee excursion, and subject height and weight, and height and weight alone predict preferred-speed quasi-stiffness with about 9% average error. The regressions provide a framework for selecting subject-specific stiffness in prosthetic and exoskeletal knees that emulate biological function during stance.
animal_study: Apply the same inverse-dynamics regression framework to instrumented animal locomotion, such as treadmill-trained cats or rodents, to test whether stance-phase moment-angle linearity and the speed dependence of joint quasi-stiffness are conserved across legged mammals.
robot_sim: Implement stage-specific constant knee quasi-stiffness slopes from the regressions in a prosthesis, exoskeleton, or neuromechanical simulation; removing the stiffness emulation quantifies its contribution to stance behavior.
flags: Tagged 'Biomechanically mediated preflexive feedback' for the stance-phase knee quasi-stiffness (linear moment-angle relation), although the abstract does not use preflex framing - drop the tag if that is too liberal.

notes: In humans running on a treadmill, sural-nerve stimulation at twice perception threshold produced reflex ratios in biceps femoris and tibialis anterior far larger than during matched isometric contractions in standing, because large facilitatory responses were present through most of the step cycle but rarely during standing contractions, while at the end of swing the responses became predominantly suppressive. Cutaneous reflex transmission is thus strongly gated by locomotor state and phase rather than by contraction level alone.
animal_study: Test the state dependence in reduced animal preparations by stimulating a cutaneous nerve at all cycle phases during standing, walking, and running analogs to separate contraction-level gating from locomotor-state gating of the facilitation.
robot_sim: Implement phase- and speed-dependent cutaneous reflex gains, facilitatory through most of the cycle and suppressive at end of swing, on a simulated runner; ablating the gating should reproduce standing-like small, suppressive responses.

notes: Chronic spinal cats generate three distinctly different fictive motor patterns, locomotion, paw shake (approximately 8 Hz rhythmic activity), and slow rhythmic leg flexion, depending only on the site and mode of stimulation (perineal skin, water jet to the paw, paw squeeze), with clonidine facilitating evocation. Passive leg movement from extension to flexion progressively shortened flexor bursts, lengthened the cycle period, and made the pattern harder to evoke, and trained late-spinal animals expressed more complex, position-dependent patterns than untrained early-spinal ones, demonstrating position-related afferent regulation of the pattern generator below a chronic transection.
animal_study: Dorsal-root section or selective deafferentation in chronic spinal cats during fictive recording would isolate which afferent channels carry the leg-position influence on flexor burst duration and cycle period.
robot_sim: Build a pattern generator supporting multiple coexistent fictive modes (stepping, paw shake, rhythmic flexion) switched by input site, and modulate flexor burst termination by a position-related afferent signal to reproduce the effects of passively moving the legs from extension to flexion.
flags: Tagged 'Fictive locomotion without sensory feedback' for the paralyzed chronic-spinal fictive preparation; rhythms were evoked by cutaneous (perineal/paw) stimulation, and the leg-position afferent class modulating burst timing is not named.

notes: In isolated neonatal mouse spinal cords, low-threshold afferents produce short-latency monosynaptic excitatory responses in most Hb9 interneurons, with VGLUT1- and parvalbumin-immunoreactive afferent contacts on somata and dendrites, and afferent input resets neurochemically induced locomotor-like rhythms: flexor-related afferent stimulation during the flexor phase delays subsequent cycle onsets while extensor-related stimulation prolongs cycle period two- to threefold, with Hb9 IN oscillations remaining phase-locked to motor bursts throughout. Hb9 INs are therefore sensorimotor interneurons positioned to regulate the pattern of locomotor rhythms.
animal_study: Ablate or silence Hb9 interneurons, for example by targeted lesion in Hb9:eGFP mice, during drug-induced locomotor-like activity to test whether afferent-induced cycle resetting is lost while the rhythm itself persists.
robot_sim: Add an Hb9 interneuron layer receiving monosynaptic afferent input and phase-locked to motor bursts in a CPG model; ablating the layer should remove the afferent phase-resetting effects on cycle timing without abolishing rhythmicity.
flags: Abstract specifies only 'low-threshold, presumably muscle afferents' (no Ia/II dissociation), so afferents left empty; the demonstrated monosynaptic excitation of Hb9 interneurons and phase-dependent cycle resetting fit no exact feedback vocabulary entry.

notes: Review arguing that state-dependent modulation of spinal reflex transmission is an investigative tool for interneuron organization: stable CNS states produced by spinal and supraspinal lesions or l-DOPA revealed previously unsuspected pathways from the flexor reflex afferents, and fictive locomotion and scratching uncovered oligosynaptic excitatory and inhibitory reflex pathways from cutaneous and muscle afferents that appear only in the flexion or extension phase. Phase-specific appearance of reflex pathways implies distinct interneuron sets with remarkably precise input/output relations.
animal_study: Systematically combine lesion- or drug-induced CNS states with phase-triggered afferent stimulation during fictive locomotion and scratching to map state- and phase-dependent interneuron circuits as the review prescribes.
robot_sim: Represent reflex pathways as state- and phase-switched interneuron banks in a locomotor model; switching network state should reveal or hide specific reflex routes, mirroring the review's examples of previously hidden pathways.
flags: Abstract names no species (classic lesion/l-DOPA/FRA experiments implied), so animals left empty; the phase-gated oligosynaptic reflex pathways described have no one-to-one feedback vocabulary entries.

notes: First characterization of putative CPG interneurons in the mammalian cord: descending-projecting L2 and L3 commissural interneurons in neonatal rats form a heterogeneous population firing in all phases of the locomotor cycle, with rhythmic dCINs in-phase with either ipsilateral or contralateral L2 activity and segregated by dorsoventral location. Their locomotor membrane oscillations arise predominantly from synaptic input with little contribution from intrinsic pacemaker currents, and the dominant synaptic drive is in-phase with ipsilateral motor activity, demonstrating anatomically and physiologically separable CPG subpopulations that can be individually targeted.
animal_study: Record from or genetically target the dorsoventrally segregated dCIN subpopulations during NMDA/5-HT-induced locomotor-like activity to test their causal roles in left-right coordination.
robot_sim: Implement left-right coordination through synaptically driven commissural interneuron populations (ipsi-phase and contra-phase) rather than intrinsic pacemakers; ablating each subpopulation tests the functional separation of coordination control.

notes: In awake walking cats, four of five broad bifunctional thigh muscles contain intramuscular subregions that are differentially recruited across locomotion, scratching, and paw shaking, and low-threshold cutaneous afferents subdivide the same muscles, but with muscle-subregion-specific and often complex responses that do not simply follow the background locomotor synergies. Cutaneous reflex premotoneuronal circuitry is therefore not synonymous with the locomotor CPG even though the two systems interact powerfully, implying specialized convergence onto task-dependent muscle subunits.
animal_study: Stimulate low-threshold cutaneous nerves at all locomotor phases while recording intramuscular subregions, before and after spinalization, to dissociate CPG-driven subdivision from reflex-pathway subdivision of bifunctional muscles.
robot_sim: Model bifunctional muscles as multiple subregion pools with task-dependent recruitment and subregion-specific cutaneous reflex gains; removing the reflex subdivision tests whether locomotor synergies alone reproduce the observed activation patterns.

notes: Reticulospinal-mediated calcium responses in lumbar motoneurons are reduced by mephenesin and by midline lesions, and stimulation in medial or lateral medullary reticular formation activates roughly half of ipsilateral and of contralateral descending commissural interneurons, with the responsive populations largely overlapping spatially. Differential descending control of trunk and hindlimb muscles by the medullary reticulospinal system is therefore mediated in part by identifiable dCIN populations, providing a polysynaptic crossed and uncrossed route to lumbar motor pools.
animal_study: Selectively stimulate or silence the dCIN subpopulations that respond to medial versus lateral medullary reticular formation while recording motoneuron responses, to test their sufficiency for differential trunk versus hindlimb control.
robot_sim: Route reticulospinal drive to bilateral motoneuron pools through a commissural interneuron layer; ablating the layer (modeling mephenesin or midline lesion) should reduce motoneuron response magnitude as observed.

notes: In decorticate cats, all studied hindlimb muscles show alpha-gamma coactivation, pure flexors and extensors alternate simply, and bifunctional pluriarticular muscles receive both flexor and extensor commands, dividing the locomotor cycle into a flexion phase, an extension phase, and two transition phases. The relative weight of these excitations depends on interactions between central commands and peripheral inflow, especially afferents acting according to the flexor reflex pattern, providing a scheme whereby an initially simple rhythmic command plus afferent gating produces the biomechanically adapted movement.
animal_study: Repeat the paper's own manipulations, exteroceptive stimulation versus curarization and deafferentation, while recording bifunctional muscle motoneurons to quantify how peripheral inflow reshapes transition-phase activity and flexor/extensor command balance.
robot_sim: Implement bifunctional motoneuron pools receiving weighted flexor and extensor CPG commands modulated by flexor-reflex-pattern afferent input; the model should generate transition-phase complexity and task-adapted output from a simple alternating rhythm.
flags: Alpha-gamma coactivation and FRA-pattern gating of bifunctional motoneurons have no exact feedback vocabulary entries; feedback left empty.

notes: Review establishing neuromodulators as constitutive components of CPG function: modulators set the parameters of CPG neurons and synapses to render the networks functional, exert multiple potentially self-stabilizing opposing effects, determine the active neuronal composition as state changes such as locomotor speed, and control the gene expression that sets each neuron's electrophysiological personality. Network models that omit neuromodulator action cannot capture CPG function or its state-dependent flexibility.
animal_study: Apply and wash out individual neuromodulators during fictive locomotion while tracking identified neurons, to test the predicted changes in active cellular composition and in synaptic parameters across speed states.
robot_sim: Implement neuromodulation as parameter control over gains, synapses, and recruited composition in a CPG model; ablating it should remove state-dependent gait flexibility, and modulators with opposing effects can be used to test the stabilization hypothesis.

notes: Formal stability analysis combined with templates yields testable hypotheses of function: because legged animals are dynamically coupled, with different passive recovery rates in different directions, reflex corrections in one direction can introduce perturbations in others, so animals should exert less neural control in directions that recover rapidly via passive dynamics (body orientation, rotation) and more in slowly or non-recovering directions (forward velocity, heading). Neural control best enhances stability when it works with the natural passive dynamics of the musculo-skeletal system, and animals appear overbuilt for steady locomotion, so perturbation experiments are the way to reveal the function of all their parts.
animal_study: Apply controlled multidirectional perturbations during locomotion and measure passive recovery rates versus active neural correction per direction, testing the hypothesized allocation of neural control to slowly recovering degrees of freedom.
robot_sim: On a template model such as SLIP, compare perturbation recovery with and without reflex correction to quantify cross-direction coupling introduced by feedback, and allocate control only to slow-recovering directions as hypothesized.

notes: Symmetry-factored return maps yield an exact algebraic necessary condition for asymptotic stability (and a sufficient condition for instability) of fixed points in 2DoF and 3DoF spring-loaded inverted pendulum models, despite the non-integrability of the SLIP dynamics. The expression characterizes analytically the sensory cost and stabilizing benefit of feedback schemes previously proposed for the 2DoF SLIP model of running and extends to a 3DoF descriptive model of the robot RHex.
robot_sim: Apply the symmetry-factored return-map analysis to a hybrid legged model's dynamics to rank candidate feedback schemes by stabilizing benefit per sensory cost before implementing any of them in a controller.

notes: During spontaneous fictive locomotion in decerebrate cats, group I afferents from the plantaris (ankle extensor) nerve always reset the locomotor rhythm, prolonging extension when stimulated in extension and terminating flexion to initiate extension when stimulated in flexion, whereas hip muscle nerve stimulation (rectus femoris, caudal gluteal, sartorius) reset the rhythm only in restricted epochs, with sartorius, particularly at group II strength, shortening the flexion phase. The epoch-specific access of hip afferents implies the rhythm generator operates with several subdivisions to determine phase and cycle durations.
animal_study: Selective section or stimulation of individual afferent classes in the plantaris and sartorius nerves during fictive locomotion would dissociate which fiber groups produce the always-resetting versus epoch-restricted effects on the rhythm generator.
robot_sim: Implement a rhythm generator with phase subdivisions such that extensor group I input prolongs extension and terminates flexion globally while hip afferent input acts only within specific phase windows; ablating the subdivision should make hip afferents reset the rhythm globally.
flags: Nerve stimuli given at group I/group II strength without Ia-vs-Ib dissociation (afferents tagged Ia, Ib, and II to reflect the fiber classes engaged); demonstrated transitions - plantaris group I prolongs extension and terminates flexion, sartorius group II shortens flexion - have no exact feedback vocabulary entry, consider adding 'group I swing to stance'.

notes: In individuals with spinal cord injury stepping on a treadmill with body-weight support, EMG mean amplitudes increased and burst durations shortened as treadmill speed rose from 0.27 to 1.52 m/s, and these modulations could not be accounted for by muscle stretch of an individual muscle and were similar in subjects with partial and with no detectable supraspinal input. The human spinal cord can therefore interpret complex, step-related, velocity-dependent afferent information to contribute to the neural control of stepping.
animal_study: Speed-series stepping in spinalized animals with and without selective dorsal-root section would identify the afferent fibers carrying the velocity-dependent modulation of EMG amplitude and burst duration.
robot_sim: Couple motoneuron burst amplitude and duration in a stepping model to cycle-velocity-dependent afferent signals rather than instantaneous muscle stretch; removing the velocity pathway should abolish the speed adaptation of motor output.
flags: The velocity-dependent afferent class is not named in the abstract; afferents left empty.

notes: Genetic ablation of V2a ipsilateral interneurons disrupts consistent left-right alternation in the mammalian spinal cord and increases locomotor burst variability while leaving flexor-extensor coordination unaffected, and anatomical tracing shows V2a cells provide direct excitatory input onto commissural interneurons, including molecularly defined V0 neurons that drive alternation. The neural substrate for left-right coordination therefore consists of at least two components: commissural neurons and a class of ipsilateral interneurons that activates commissural pathways.
animal_study: The ablation model itself is the test; recording left-right and flexor-extensor coordination across locomotor speeds in V2a-ablated animals would establish whether the ipsilateral relay onto commissural pathways is speed-dependent.
robot_sim: Implement an ipsilateral V2a excitatory relay onto commissural (V0-like) cross-coupling in a left-right CPG; ablating the relay should selectively degrade left-right alternation while preserving flexor-extensor timing on each side.

notes: In chronic spinal cats walking on a treadmill, tactile stimulation of the paw dorsum during swing evokes a short-latency flexion response with concomitant crossed extension, while the same stimulus during stance increases ipsilateral extension, a phase-dependent reflex reversal that compensates for unpredicted obstacles by lifting the paw in swing and reinforcing support in stance. The responses are well adapted to ongoing locomotion and leave interlimb coordination intact, except when delivered as the foot approaches the ground after flexion, where the alternating pattern is disturbed.
animal_study: Map the phase dependence with dense cycle-phase stimulation of the paw dorsum before and after additional spinal lesions to localize where the swing-versus-stance reversal of the tactile reflex is gated.
robot_sim: Implement a phase-switched paw-dorsum cutaneous reflex, flexion plus crossed extension in swing and ipsilateral extension reinforcement in stance, in a walking model; ablating it tests its contribution to obstacle compensation.

notes: In neonatal mouse brainstem-spinal cord preparations, pontine reticulospinal stimulation activates axial and limb motoneurons bilaterally at cervical, thoracic, and lumbar levels, similarly in medial and lateral motor columns and in flexor- and extensor-dominant segments, with responses following individual stimuli in trains nearly one-to-one. Unilateral C1 hemisection separates two pathways, an uncrossed one that transmits more faithfully and appears more direct, and a crossed one with smaller, longer-latency responses, defining a dual-route organization for bilateral descending control of trunk and limb motor pools.
animal_study: Additional lesions at successive segmental levels combined with optical motoneuron recording would localize the synaptic relays of the crossed versus uncrossed pontine reticulospinal pathways.
robot_sim: Model descending pontine drive as parallel fast-uncrossed and slower-crossed routes to bilateral motoneuron pools; sectioning the crossed route should reproduce the longer latencies and stimulus-train failures seen after contralateral hemisection.

notes: In cats receiving staggered thoracic lateral hemisections on opposite sides of the cord, short-latency cutaneous reflex responses from superficial peroneal stimulation were largely preserved in homonymous and crossed hindlimb muscles, while mid- and long-latency homonymous and crossed responses in both hindlimbs, and forelimb responses, occurred less frequently; whenever responses were present, all latency classes retained their phase-dependent modulation. Loss of longer-latency cutaneous transmission therefore tracks impaired balance and interlimb coordination after spinal cord injury, making reflex transmission a candidate biomarker for locomotor recovery.
animal_study: The staggered-hemisection model with bilateral nerve stimulation is the paradigm; adding training or pharmacological interventions while tracking short-, mid-, and long-latency reflex recovery would test the biomarker proposal.
robot_sim: Implement short-, mid-, and long-latency cutaneous reflex arcs with phase-dependent gating in a quadruped model; ablating the long-latency inter-enlargement transmission should degrade interlimb coordination while sparing short-latency responses.
